source_evidence.anchor: “real eigenvalues and a corresponding set of m linearly independent eigenvectors”
source_evidence.observation: A constant-coefficient system is called hyperbolic when its coefficient matrix has real eigenvalues and a complete independent eigenvector set. Vectors in R^m then have unique eigenvector decompositions, with eigenvalues giving wave speeds.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF pages 25–26; printed pages 3–4; Section 1.1, equations (1.8)–(1.9) and continuation
source_evidence.anchor: q_t(x,t) + f(q(x,t))_x = 0; q_t + f′(q)q_x = 0; f(q) = Aq
source_evidence.observation: The source presents a one-dimensional conservation law, calls f its flux function, and connects nonlinear hyperbolicity to the flux Jacobian satisfying the preceding matrix conditions. The linear system corresponds to the linear flux Aq; nonlinear conservation laws use a nonlinear flux of the conserved-quantity vector q.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; Section 1.1.1, equation (1.10) and following paragraph
source_evidence.observation: For any two endpoints, the interval integral changes through the physical endpoint fluxes. Each component of q measures the density of a conserved quantity. The text separately notes that nonconserved quantities require source terms.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF pages 26–27; printed pages 4–5; Section 1.1.2
source_evidence.anchor: “provided that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth”; “does continue to hold”
source_evidence.observation: Derivation of the classical differential equation from integral conservation requires sufficient smoothness. Discontinuities can develop even from smooth initial data; at a discontinuity the classical PDE fails, while the integral conservation law remains fundamental and continues to hold.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.2, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: “the cell average of q”; “modified in each time step by the flux through the edges”
source_evidence.observation: Finite volume methods approximate cell integrals or cell averages. The cell average is the integral divided by cell volume. Time-step updates use cell-edge fluxes, and numerical flux functions approximate the correct fluxes using the available approximate cell averages.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.2.1, equation (1.11) and following paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: q(x,0) = q_l for x < 0, q_r for x > 0; q_l = Q_(i−1), q_r = Q_i
source_evidence.observation: A Riemann problem combines the hyperbolic equation with piecewise constant initial data having a single jump. Neighboring cell averages provide its left and right states, and its solution supplies information for computing numerical fluxes and updating averages.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; continuation of Section 1.2.1
source_evidence.observation: The source explains that exact nonlinear Riemann solutions are often computationally expensive, motivating approximate Riemann solvers in numerical implementations.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; Section 1.2.2, second paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: “capture discontinuities in the solution automatically”; “not introduce nonphysical oscillations”
source_evidence.observation: Shock capturing aims to represent discontinuities without explicit tracking. The stated success criteria include correct jump conditions, minimal smearing, and avoidance of nonphysical oscillations; high-resolution finite volume methods based on Riemann solutions often perform well.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 125; printed page 103; Section 6.3, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: “Second-order accuracy is obtained where possible”; “we don’t insist on it”
source_evidence.observation: High-resolution methods aim to combine the smooth-solution accuracy of second-order methods with the monotone behavior associated with upwind methods. The source explicitly relaxes the second-order objective where the solution is not smooth.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF pages 125–126; printed pages 103–104; Section 6.3, equation (6.9) and its following discussion
source_evidence.anchor: “applying some form of limiter”; “each wave limited independently from the others”
source_evidence.observation: The source describes limiting a correction to an upwind flux according to solution behavior. For systems, characteristic structure allows correction terms based on Riemann waves to be limited independently, with the aim of retaining accuracy in smooth portions and nonoscillatory behavior in discontinuous portions.
